video_title: Steven Tananbaum: The Evolution of Credit Investing and AI Opportunities
gist: GoldenTree founder/CIO Steve Tananbaum (>$70bn AUM) tells Goldman's John Waldron that the main AI risk for credit is not AI defaults but a deceleration of AI spend forcing down economy-wide growth assumptions, while AI-related supply is already pushing investment-grade spreads 8-10bp wider (SpaceX 50-60bp) even though AI is only ~2% of the below-investment-grade index. He lays out a distressed 1.0/2.0/3.0 framework, hard margin-of-safety guardrails (2x asset coverage senior, 1.5x junior), and the anatomy of trades that made ~$3bn in European banks, ~$1.5bn in Covid-era oil service and $800m in directories at a 1.5x EV entry price.

insights.claim: Tananbaum's biggest AI worry for credit is not AI-company defaults but macro deceleration: AI is such a large driver of the economy that it is hard to see it accelerating from here, and if it decelerates, investors will have to mark down their economic growth assumptions.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: The credit trade to watch is not AI issuer spreads but a broad growth-assumption reset; position for cyclical, not idiosyncratic, AI risk.
insights.quote: hard to see how it's going to actually accelerate

insights.claim: AI-related financings are only about 2% of the below-investment-grade index and have been funded mostly in investment grade, so the high yield index is far less directly exposed to AI capex than headlines imply.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Screening AI credit exposure through HY indices understates it; the concentration sits in IG and private credit instead.
insights.quote: It's only about 2% in below investment grade.

insights.claim: AI financing supply is already pressuring the investment-grade market, with spreads out eight to ten basis points in the past week alone, according to Tananbaum.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: IG spread widening is being driven by technical supply from AI issuance, not deteriorating credit — a mispricing that creates entry points.
insights.quote: And it's already pressuring that market. You see

insights.claim: SpaceX debt has already widened by roughly 50-60 basis points, which Tananbaum flags as one of the easier opportunities being created by AI-driven issuance pressure.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Names widening on supply technicals rather than fundamentals — SpaceX cited by name — are the first place to look for cheap AI-adjacent credit.

insights.claim: Tananbaum thinks the investment-grade market, not high yield or equity, could be the better risk-adjusted opportunity precisely because AI financing pressure has widened it.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: A $70bn credit CIO pointing at IG over HY is a rotation signal within credit allocations.
insights.quote: the better risk-adjusted opportunity

insights.claim: AI spend is being financed wherever product demand is greatest — split across structured product, corporate debt, private credit and the equity market — so aggregate AI leverage is not visible in any single index.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Measuring AI financing risk requires summing across public IG, structured and private credit channels; single-market exposure metrics will understate it.

insights.claim: Tananbaum would 'be shocked' if AI-driven disruption did not produce more dispersion in credit markets, and says he would give odds on it.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Rising dispersion favors security-selection and long/short credit strategies over index beta.
insights.quote: I would be shocked if we didn't see more

insights.claim: The instinct at every technology inflection — including AI now — is to price disruption too broadly across all potentially affected sectors, which is what created the 2000-era TMT opportunity set.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Indiscriminate AI-disruption selling should throw up mispriced 'losers' whose cash flows survive far longer than the market assumes.

insights.claim: Internet disruption of advertising took four to five years to actually hit newspapers (only really biting by 2005-2006), and cable programmers stayed a terrific industry for another 15 years despite being 'impacted' — the timing gap between identified disruption and realized impairment is where credit money is made.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: For AI-disrupted issuers, short-dated debt can still money-good for years even when the equity story is over; match maturity to the real impairment clock.
insights.quote: around four or five years to really get going,

insights.claim: Telesystems International, a hodgepodge of international cellular stakes, traded down to 30 cents on the dollar in 2000 purely on fear that financing would be unavailable; GoldenTree cut a deal at 70 cents and the assets sold the following year for significantly more than the debt.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Financing-availability panic, not asset quality, is the recurring source of the deepest credit discounts — the same setup to hunt in an AI funding squeeze.
insights.quote: names like TMT, like Telesystems International.

insights.claim: Tananbaum's analog framework says that when you start a year mid-cycle with tight spreads and expected growth above 2%, credit on average does poorly and equities do very well — and that is exactly how the year has played out through July.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: A reusable regime screen: mid-cycle plus tight plus >2% growth argues for equity over credit beta; deviations from it flag a regime change.

insights.claim: GoldenTree treats cable as a viable business under siege from streaming and broadband competition and chooses expression by best risk-adjusted route — a large distressed cable name versus the public company — rather than defaulting to one asset class.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Theme identification and instrument selection are separate decisions; the same cable view can be expressed at very different risk-adjusted prices.
insights.quote: cable is very much under siege. There are concerns

insights.claim: In Argentina, buying province debt rather than sovereign debt has offered better upside participation and better downside protection: it is less liquid and trades cheaper, but has historically had materially better recoveries in restructurings.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: A specific, still-live EM trade: sub-sovereign Argentine paper as a cheaper, better-protected substitute for the crowded sovereign that has already run hard for two years.
insights.quote: province debt, which is less liquid, but in all

insights.claim: GoldenTree deliberately built permanent capability in structured products, real estate and emerging markets rather than being a 'situation tourist,' because edges like the Argentine province-versus-sovereign recovery differential are invisible without a dedicated team.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Sourcing edge in credit is increasingly an organizational-capability question, which favors large multi-strategy credit platforms over opportunistic single-strategy funds.
insights.quote: everlasting opposed to being a situation tourist

insights.claim: Distressed 1.0 — the RJR Nabisco-style trade of simply changing the debt/equity mix to capture a balance-sheet arbitrage — no longer exists as an evergreen strategy and now appears only cyclically, as it did during Covid and in Q4 2015.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Allocators underwriting distressed managers on classic capital-structure arbitrage are buying a cyclical, not structural, return stream.
insights.quote: And for the most part that doesn't really exist

insights.claim: Distressed 2.0 is fixing broken execution rather than broken balance sheets — replacing management, changing the board and installing accountability — and Tananbaum expects to see a lot of it in the current crop of LBOs where management did not do what they were supposed to.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: A forward signal that the recent LBO vintage will generate governance-driven restructurings; watch sponsor-owned credits with execution shortfalls.
insights.quote: And you're going to see that a lot on some of the

insights.claim: Distressed 3.0 — owning a platform and using cyclical downturns to buy companies and industries going through transformation — has the largest moat of the three, and GoldenTree is running it now through Superior Energy in oil service.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Names an active, disclosed platform position (Superior Energy) and identifies where the durable distressed alpha now sits — consolidation platforms, not paper trades.
insights.quote: the most exciting part of distressed is when you

insights.claim: Tananbaum underwrites distressed positions to a desirable exit from day one — asking what makes the company attractive to a potential acquirer — because a balance-sheet fix plus better management and responsible directors alone does not get you there.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Exit design, not just recovery math, distinguishes returns in post-reorg equity; assess whether a restructuring produces a sellable asset.
insights.quote: that's not getting you there.

themes.theme: Entry Price Discipline and Avoiding Value Traps

insights.claim: Tananbaum says the recurring failure in distressed investing is that people debate the prospects of the business and never discuss the entry price, which is the actual determinant of whether a cheap-looking asset is a value trap.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: A screening rule: reject any distressed thesis whose case rests on business improvement rather than on the multiple paid at entry.
insights.quote: How did we do that? Our entry price.

insights.claim: GoldenTree made $800 million with high-20s returns in the directory industry — a visibly shrinking business full of Chapter 22s and 33s — by buying at an average entry of 1.5x enterprise value.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Proof that terminal-decline industries can be the highest-return credit trades if entered at ~1.5x EV; applies directly to today's AI-disrupted secular losers.
insights.quote: We made $800 million on the directory

insights.claim: In dying industries Tananbaum deliberately backs management teams committed to returning capital and explicitly discourages reinvention spending, telling one Canadian directory management team not to spend money reinventing themselves and to liquidate in front of the decline instead.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Management's capital-allocation intent is a screenable variable in secular decliners: reinvestment attempts with uncertain success rates destroy creditor recoveries.
insights.quote: with management teams that were returning capital

themes.theme: Anatomy of the Big Trades: European Banks and Oil Service

insights.claim: The BAWAG investment was underwritten on a modest premise — a high single-digit return on equity that might reach 12%, at which point you could exit at book value for a primarily retail bank — and it beat that badly, going to mid-teens return on tangible equity.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Illustrates underwriting to a conservative exit-at-book premise and letting upside be free optionality — the template for recapitalization equity.
insights.quote: do a round, a high single digit return on equity.

insights.claim: GoldenTree extrapolated the BAWAG insight across European banks in the late 2010s when the sector earned ~10% return on tangible capital while trading at 60% of tangible book, betting against a consensus that the books were mismarked without evidence — and earned about $3 billion on the theme.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: The pattern to copy: when a sector trades far below book solely on an unevidenced belief that marks are wrong, the disproof event (no write-downs) is the re-rating catalyst.
insights.quote: And so, we on that theme earned about $3 billion.

insights.claim: Covid validated European bank marks because the banks took no write-downs, and simultaneously rising rates in a stable economy lifted sector return on equity from ~9-10% to 14-15%, moving the shares from 60% of tangible book to well above book.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: The bank re-rating was driven by rates plus proof-of-marks; a rate-cutting cycle with a stable economy removes half that engine.
insights.quote: is very good for banks.

insights.claim: Being invested in BAWAG gave GoldenTree an information edge on the ECB, which they found to be a much better advocate and partner to banks than press coverage suggested — the insight they then extrapolated across the European banking sector.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Regulator posture, learned from inside a position, is an underpriced variable in bank capital-structure investing.
insights.quote: was a much better advocate and partner than maybe

insights.claim: In spring 2020 GoldenTree bought onshore and offshore oil service companies at a 70% discount to their reasonable normalized earnings capability and an 80-90% discount to replacement value, became probably the largest owner of offshore rigs on a consolidated basis, and made about $1.5 billion.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: The replacement-value plus normalized-earnings double discount is the screen that identified the trade; look for the same setup wherever a shock temporarily zeroes an end market.
insights.quote: oil service companies as a 70% discount to what

themes.theme: Process, Risk Guardrails and Behavioral Edge

insights.claim: GoldenTree's process starts with hard margin-of-safety guardrails rather than analysis: two times asset coverage (50% loan-to-value) for senior debt and 1.5 times asset coverage for junior debt.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable underwriting floor for private and stressed credit — and a benchmark to judge whether today's private credit deals clear it.
insights.quote: So, we start with providing a margin of safety.

insights.claim: GoldenTree explicitly rejects large, exhaustive investment memos in favor of identifying the five or six issues that drive an outcome plus the mosaic needed to confirm them, and treats a thesis that is hard to track or confirm as an allocation-sizing question rather than a reason to pass.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Confirmability of a thesis, not conviction in it, sets position size — a practical rule for sizing under uncertainty.
insights.quote: what are the five things or six things that make

insights.claim: After seven strong or average years, 2008 was GoldenTree's first genuinely bad year and exposed inadequate risk management; Tananbaum's bet was that peers would not make the same corrections, so surviving to 2010 in better shape would leave the firm differentiated.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Drawdown response, not drawdown avoidance, is the manager-selection variable; ask what a manager structurally changed after their worst year.
insights.quote: 2008, really poor year. It was very humbling.

insights.claim: Reviewing his career, Tananbaum concluded he had consistently been a seller too early, and because 2008-2009 underwriting was materially better than prior vintages he stayed risk-on after passing his high-water mark in October 2009 — producing a 24% year in 2010.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Crisis-vintage underwriting quality justifies holding risk longer than instinct suggests; spreads swing from very wide to very tight, and selling into the first recovery leg forfeits most of the return.
insights.quote: I probably was a seller too early.

insights.claim: Tananbaum's edge came from watching how other portfolio managers actually behave rather than how they logically should: on outflows he sold the hardest-to-move paper first while others sold their most liquid holdings, and post-crisis he lifted offers to 86 cents because CLOs got far better credit for loans at 86 than at 82, so that is where the liquidity was.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Rules-based buyers (CLO tests, fund liquidity policies) create predictable price points where liquidity clusters — a repeatable execution edge in loans.
insights.quote: But if I sold it at 86 cents, you got much higher

insights.claim: Tananbaum's original alpha source at MacKay Shields was applying earnings momentum to credit — betting bonds rise when earnings beat market expectations — combined with buying stressed names below intrinsic value, which took a portfolio ranked 89th of 91 to number one in three years.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Equity-style earnings-revision signals are still under-applied in credit; the historical proof of concept is this track record.
insights.quote: It's ranked 89th out of 91.

themes.theme: Building a Credit Franchise and Collecting Art

insights.claim: Tananbaum launched GoldenTree in 2000 on an explicit supply/demand read: growth equity had roughly 100 top-quartile managers competing for mandates while credible below-investment-grade credit managers were a much shorter list, and an anchor hedge fund investor offered to double his allocation past $100 million and double the fees if he went out on his own.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: Scarcity of genuine credit-investing skill relative to allocator demand was the founding arbitrage — the same imbalance now driving private credit fundraising.
insights.quote: size of the money, over $100 million, and double

insights.claim: For art, Tananbaum's rule is to buy established names such as Andy Warhol or Willem de Kooning (prints rather than paintings if capital is limited) and, on the primary market, only artists with roughly ten years of differentiated work behind them, as Julie Mehretu had when he first bought a drawing.
insights.speaker: Steve Tananbaum
insights.so_what: A track-record filter for an illiquid alternative asset: a decade of consistent output has best stood the test of time, and prints are the low-capital entry point.
insights.quote: with artists who we feel have had ten years of
